lesson.title: Remembering That y Is a Function of x
lesson.summary: Implicit differentiation works because you mentally treat y as an unnamed function y(x) the whole way through, which is exactly what licenses the chain rule on every y-term.
lesson.body:
Underneath the mechanics of implicit differentiation is a single mental habit: treat y as y(x), a genuine but unwritten function of x, even though the equation never spells out a formula for it. This habit is what makes the whole method legal. If you forget it, one of two wrong things tends to happen. Either you treat y like a constant, in which case d/dx[y^2] comes out to 0, which is wrong because y does change as x changes along the curve. Or you treat y like the independent variable itself, in which case d/dx[y^2] comes out to 2y with no dy/dx attached, which is wrong because that would be the derivative with respect to y, not with respect to x.

The correct move sits between those two mistakes. Because y is a function of x, differentiating any expression built out of y, whether it is y^2, sin(y), or y^3, uses the chain rule exactly the way you would differentiate f(x)^2 or sin(f(x)): differentiate the outer operation as usual, then multiply by the derivative of the inner function, which for y(x) is dy/dx.

A clean example: y^2 = x, at the point (4, 2), where 2^2 = 4 checks out. Differentiate both sides with respect to x. The left side is the chain rule case just described: d/dx[y^2] = 2y (dy/dx). The right side is d/dx[x] = 1. So 2y (dy/dx) = 1, giving dy/dx = 1/(2y). At (4, 2), dy/dx = 1/4.

Since y^2 = x solves explicitly on this branch as y = sqrt(x), you can check directly: dy/dx = 1/(2 sqrt(x)), and since sqrt(x) = y here, that is 1/(2y), the same formula, and at x = 4 it gives 1/(2 * 2) = 1/4. The general implicit differentiation technique from the previous chapter is really just this habit, treating y as a function of x, applied systematically term by term across an entire equation.
